title: Word problems at speed
objectives: Turn short word problems into arithmetic quickly.

screens.prose: A trading test asks: you buy 300 shares at £4.25 and sell them at £4.40. Before computing, write one line: 300 times the gain on each share.
screens.question: What is the profit, in pounds?

hints.text: Find the gain on one share first.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the shares by the gain on each.

byKey.sale-value: £1,320 is what the sale brings in. The profit is the sale less the £1,275 cost.
byKey.per-share: 15p is the gain on one share. There are 300 shares.

explain.text: One line, $300 \times (4.40 - 4.25)$, avoids two big products. The gain is 15p, and $300 \times 0.15 = 45$. Multiplying 300 by each price would mean £1,320 less £1,275, slower and riskier.

screens.prose: A train leaves at 14:47 and takes 2 h 38 min. Drag the point to the arrival time. The bar is the journey, and the caption converts the minutes for you.
screens.question: Drag the point to when the train arrives.

hints.text: 14:47 plus 2 hours is 16:47. Then add 38 minutes.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag until the caption reads 2 h 38 min.

byKey.hours-only: 16:47 adds the 2 hours but not the 38 minutes.
byKey.rounded: 17:47 adds 3 hours. The journey is 22 minutes short of that.
byKey.arr: Drag until the caption says 2 h 38 min, then read the arrival.

explain.text: Two hours take 14:47 to 16:47, and 38 more minutes make $47 + 38 = 85$. Eighty-five minutes is 1 h 25, so the train arrives at 17:25. Turning 85 minutes into hours is the unit change these questions hide.

screens.prose: You turned words into **one line** of arithmetic before computing. Try it on "a share rises 12%, then falls 12%". Each change is a growth factor, and the line is their product.
screens.question: Fill in the factors, the line’s product and the net change.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write each factor, then multiply.

byKey.r3c1: A factor of 0.9856 is a fall of 1.44%, not 0%. The fall acts on the higher price.

explain.text: The line $1.12 \times 0.88$ is a difference of two squares: $1 - 0.12^2 = 0.9856$. So the share ends 1.44% down. Writing the line first stops you adding +12 and −12 to get 0.

screens.prose: On 3 March a client deposits £1,250 at 4% a year, simple interest. Some numbers in the words are not in the line. Write the line before computing.
screens.question: What interest is due after 9 months, in pounds?

hints.text: A year’s interest is £50. Nine months is $\tfrac34$ of a year.

feedback.correct: £50 a year, and nine months is three quarters: £37.50.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find a year’s interest, then take $\tfrac{9}{12}$ of it.

byKey.year: £50 is a full year. The deposit earns for 9 months, so $\tfrac34$ of £50.
byKey.months-as-years: You multiplied by 9 as if it were 9 years. Nine months is $\tfrac{9}{12}$ of a year.
byKey.used-date: You used the 3 from 3 March as 3 months. The date is not in the line; the term is 9 months.

explain.text: The line is $1250 \times 0.04 \times \tfrac{9}{12}$, and the date is not in it. A year’s interest is £50, and three quarters of that is £37.50. Spotting the number that does not matter is half these questions.

screens.prose: A desk of 4 traders orders lunch: one item at £2.99, one at £4.49 and one at £7.99. Round each up to a round price, add, then take off the pennies you added.
screens.question: What is the total, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the rounded prices, then take off the 3p.

byKey.no-pence: £15.50 is the rounded sum. Each item was rounded up by 1p, so take off 3p.
byKey.times-desk: You multiplied by the 4 traders. The order is three items, one of each.
byKey.one-penny: You took off 1p. Each of the three roundings added 1p, so take off 3p.

explain.text: £3, £4.50 and £8 make £15.50. Three roundings of 1p each mean the true total is 3p less: £15.47. The 4 traders were a number in the words, not in the line.

screens.title: The follow-up
screens.prose: Back to the trade: bought 300 at £4.25, sold at £4.40, a profit of £45. The interviewer follows up: what is that as a return on the money you put in?
screens.question: What is the return on the cost, in percent?

hints.text: The money put in is the cost, £1,275.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the gain by the price you paid.

byKey.sale-price: You divided by £4.40, the sale price. A return is measured on what you paid: £4.25.
byKey.pence: You typed 0.15, the gain in pounds, as the percentage. Divide it by £4.25.

explain.text: The line is $\tfrac{0.15}{4.25}$: the share count cancels. $\tfrac{0.15}{4.25}$ is a little over $\tfrac{0.15}{4.5} = 3.33\%$, and it is 3.53%. One line again: the gain over what you paid.

screens.prose: An order to buy 2,400 shares at £3.20 is 35% filled.
screens.question: How many shares have been bought so far?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take 35% of the 2,400 shares.

byKey.left: 1,560 is the 65% still to fill. You read "35% filled" as 35% left.
byKey.price: £7,680 is the full order’s value. The question asks for shares, and the price is not in the line.
byKey.value: You found 840 shares and then multiplied by £3.20. The question asks for shares, not pounds.

explain.text: "35% filled" means 35% done: $0.35 \times 2400 = 840$. The price is in the words but not in this line. Reading filled as left gives 1,560, the most common slip.

screens.prose: Every answer came from one line, written before any arithmetic. The lines were shares times gain, a product of factors and part of a whole. Interest has its own line, with the months turned into years: $$\text{interest} = P \times \frac{r}{100} \times \frac{m}{12}$$
screens.question: £2,400 at 5% a year simple interest for 6 months: what interest is due, in pounds?

feedback.correct: £120 a year, half of it for 6 months: £60.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find a year’s interest, then take $\tfrac{6}{12}$ of it.

byKey.year: £120 is a full year. Six months is half of that.
byKey.months-as-years: You multiplied by 6 as if it were years. Divide the months by 12.

explain.text: $2400 \times 0.05 = 120$ a year, and $\tfrac{6}{12}$ of that is £60. The months-to-years step is the unit change. Leave it out and the answer is twelve times too big.

screens.prose: Write the interest line as one formula. $P$ is the deposit in pounds, $r$ the yearly rate in percent and $m$ the months. Fold the 100 and the 12 into one number.
screens.question: Simple interest equals what?

hints.text: Multiply the tops and the bottoms.

feedback.correct: $\dfrac{Prm}{1200}$: the rate turned into a fraction and the months into years.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide by 100 for the percent and by 12 for the months.

byKey.years: That treats $m$ as years. Divide the months by 12 as well.
byKey.no-percent: That leaves $r$ as a whole number. Divide by 100 for the percent.

explain.text: $P \times \tfrac{r}{100} \times \tfrac{m}{12} = \tfrac{Prm}{1200}$. Check: $\tfrac{1250 \times 4 \times 9}{1200} = 37.5$. Folding the constants once saves a step every time.

screens.title: Check your methods in code
screens.prose: Two checks for your fast methods. `minutes_between(t1, t2)` returns the minutes from one `'HH:MM'` time to the next; if `t2` is earlier, it is the next day. `simple_interest(principal, rate, months)` returns the interest in pounds.
screens.question: Complete both functions.

widget.how: Check runs 12 hidden tests: six time gaps (exact minutes, two of them past midnight) and six interest sums (`math.isclose`).

hints.text: Turn each time into minutes after midnight.
`h * 60 + m`, then subtract. `% (24 * 60)` handles the next day.

feedback.correct: Both checks agree with your fast methods.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work in minutes after midnight, and turn months into years.

explain.text: Minutes after midnight make every time a plain number. The remainder by 1,440 turns 22:35 to 02:25 into 230 minutes rather than a negative gap. The interest is the lesson’s one line, $\tfrac{Prm}{1200}$.

screens.title: Drill: ten word problems
screens.prose: Ten word problems. Target pace: 10 seconds each, 100 seconds in all. The app does not time you, so use your own watch. Write the one line in your head first. Times as HH:MM; a loss with a minus sign.
screens.question: Fill in all ten.

rows: A share rises 10%, then falls 10%: net change (%)
An order of 1,800 shares is 40% filled: shares filled
Leave 09:38; the journey takes 1 h 47 min: arrive at
£800 at 3% simple interest for 6 months: interest (£)
A 90-minute call starts at 16:45: it ends at

hints.text: Say the one line before any number.
Row 4: 38 + 47 minutes is 85, which is 1 h 25.

feedback.correct: All ten right. Note your time against the 100-second target.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Redo the amber rows from the one line.

byKey.r4c1: £24 a year; half of it is £12.

explain.text: Each row was one line: shares times gain, a factor product, a share of a whole, or minutes into hours. Rows 4, 5, 7 and 9 needed a unit change. Those are the ones to time again.

screens.prose: A trading assessment’s scenario: you quote 2,000 shares at £12.48 bid and £12.52 ask. A client buys 1,500 from you at the ask. Then the mid price moves to £12.60.
screens.question: What is your P&L on the 1,500 shares, marked at the new mid, in pounds?

hints.text: The client bought, so you sold: you are short 1,500.
You sold at £12.52, and they are now worth £12.60: 8p against you.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. You sold 1,500 at £12.52; mark them at £12.60.

byKey.quote-size: You used the 2,000 quoted. Only 1,500 traded.
byKey.sign: You sold, and the price rose, so it is a loss: −£120.
byKey.bid: You sold at the ask, £12.52, not the bid. The move against you is 8p, not 12p.

explain.text: The line is $1500 \times (12.52 - 12.60) = -120$. The 2,000 and the £12.48 are in the story but not in the line. Scenario questions test exactly that reading, at speed.

ideas: Write one line of arithmetic before computing: shares × gain, a product of factors, a share of a whole.
Some numbers in the words are not in the line: dates, sizes quoted, prices when shares are asked.
Watch the units: minutes carry into hours at 60, pence into pounds at 100, months into years at 12.
summary.trap: Reading "35% filled" as 35% left: 2,400 shares 35% filled is 840 bought, not 1,560.

quiz.question: What do they cost, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn 85p into £0.85 first.

byKey.pence: 102,000 is the cost in pence. Divide by 100 for pounds.

explain.text: 85p is £0.85, and $1200 \times 0.85 = 1020$. The unit change from pence to pounds is a factor of 100.

quiz.question: How many minutes does it last?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count up to the next hour, then on.

byKey.decimal: You subtracted 950 from 1,115, as if an hour had 100 minutes.

explain.text: From 09:50 to 10:00 is 10 minutes, then 1 h 15 to 11:15. That makes 85 minutes. Counting up past the hour avoids the 100-minute slip.

quiz.prose: An order for 3,600 shares is 15% filled by 10:00 and another 20% by noon.
quiz.question: How many shares are filled by noon?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the two fills, then take that share of 3,600.

byKey.left: 2,340 is the 65% still open. Filled is the part done.
byKey.first-only: 540 is the 15% by 10:00. Add the noon fill too.

explain.text: Both fills are shares of the same 3,600, so they add: 35%. And 35% of 3,600 is 1,260. The times are in the words, not the line.

quiz.prose: A bill of £84 includes VAT at 20%.
quiz.question: What was the price before VAT, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The £84 is 120% of the price.

byKey.took-20: You took 20% off £84. The VAT was 20% of the lower price, so divide by 1.2.

explain.text: £84 is 1.2 times the price, so the line is $84 \div 1.2 = 70$. Check: 20% of £70 is £14, and $70 + 14 = 84$.
